rashi:a3.1: Does the one who consecrates add one-fifth, or does the one atoning add one-fifth: for we hold (Bava Metzia 53b) that the owners add one-fifth if they redeem their consecrated item, and if others redeem it they do not add one-fifth. Therefore, if this person separated an offering for the atonement of his fellow and it became blemished, who are its owners, so that if he redeems it he adds one-fifth? Is the one who consecrates the owner, while the one atoning is like another person and does not add? Or is the one atoning its owner?
rashi:a4.1: If so: that the one who consecrates effects substitution, we find substitution by the community and by partners. How so? For example, where the community or partners appointed an agent to consecrate an offering on their behalf, for now the one consecrating is an individual, and it is called an individual’s offering, if we go by him. But we learned at the end of our chapter’s mishnayot (13a) that the community and partners do not effect substitution. Rather, we go by the one atoning; therefore their offering does not effect substitution, since many achieve atonement through it and it is not called an individual’s offering. And we derive below from the animal tithe that an individual’s offering effects substitution, but not that of the community and partners.
tosafot:a4.1: Rava said: If so: meaning, if the one who consecrates effects substitution, we find the community and partners effecting substitution, for example where they appointed an agent to consecrate it. But we cannot argue the reverse, that if the one atoning effects substitution we would find the community and partners effecting substitution, for example where they consecrated an animal for an individual to atone with: since an individual atones with it, it is not the community’s but an individual’s.
rashi:a5.1: Means: that is a sliding-scale offering [whose kind depends on what one can afford]. But the nazirite’s offering is fixed, whether he is rich or poor!
rashi:a5.2: How so: this is what the verse is saying: “his offering” that he separated from his own he shall bring for his vow; “besides that for which his means suffice”: besides that, if he cannot separate one from his own because he is poor, and later his means suffice in that others give him one, he may bring that too and fulfill his obligation.
rashi:a6.1: With regard to atonement: to teach us that he can atone with an animal that someone else separated for his need.
rashi:a6.2: [Rashi’s text reads:] Just as when he separated it from his own, he effects substitution with it and not another person, so too when others separated it for him, he effects substitution with it and not another person.
rashi:a7.1: Only from his own does he atone: as it is written: “His offering unto the Lord.”
rashi:a9.1: The benefit of discretion is his: the separator’s. The benefit of discretion is in his hand, to give it to whichever priest he wishes, and not in the hand of the one on whose behalf he separated it.
rashi:a9.2: As it is written: “All the tithe” etc.: “When you have made an end of tithing” etc. This implies that whoever takes the tithe from produce in his own hand may give it to whomever he wishes, and it is not in the hand of his fellow on whose behalf it was separated. The benefit of discretion is a small sum that he receives from an Israelite on condition that he give all his terumot to that man’s daughter’s son, who is a priest.
rashi:a10.1: MISHNA: Not limbs: of non-sacred animals for fetuses of consecrated animals. That if he said: Let the leg of this animal be a substitute for the consecrated fetus in the womb of this animal, the sanctity does not take effect on the limb.
rashi:a10.2: And not fetuses for limbs: that if he said: The fetus in the womb of this non-sacred animal is a substitute for the leg of this consecrated animal, the fetus is not sacred.
rashi:a10.3: Nor limbs and fetuses: of non-sacred animals, for whole consecrated animals.
rashi:a10.4: Nor whole animals: non-sacred ones, for limbs and fetuses of consecrated animals.
rashi:a11.1: One substitutes limbs for whole animals: if he said: The leg of this non-sacred animal is a substitute in place of this consecrated animal, the substitution takes effect on the limb and spreads through the whole animal, and all of it is a substitute and is sacrificed.
rashi:a11.2: But not whole animals for them: for one limb of a consecrated animal has no power to effect substitution.
rashi:a11.3: But isn’t it so with regard to sacrificial animals: that is, at the start of consecration, when he consecrates it, if he said: Its leg is a burnt offering, [all of it is a burnt offering,] as the reason is explained below in the Gemara.
rashi:a12.1: GEMARA: Sanctity does not take effect on fetuses: if he consecrated a fetus in an animal’s womb, it is not sacred to be sacrificed. And if he sacrifices it when it is born and did not consecrate it once born, he is bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple courtyard. And if he set aside a pregnant animal as a sin offering, they are not like two sin offerings set aside as a guarantee [one in case the other is lost], for the fetus is sacred by force of its mother and not by its own force; it is like the offspring of a sin offering and goes to its death. And so in all its matters it is like the offspring of consecrated animals, and not like an original consecration.
rashi:a12.2: If he wishes he may achieve atonement through its offspring: for when we say that the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death, that is where he separated his sin offering and it then became pregnant and gave birth. For the five sin offerings that are left to die are a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai, and this is how it was received, that such an offspring dies. But if he separated it while pregnant, the fetus counts as another animal, and the sanctity takes effect on it in its own right. It is like one who separates two sin offerings as a guarantee, who atones with whichever he wishes, and the other is left to graze. Evidently sanctity takes effect on fetuses.
tosafot:a12.1: It was stated: Bar Padda: this is bar Padda, the son of bar Kappara’s sister, as it is found in the first chapter of Me’ila (4b): “Bar Kappara said to bar Padda, his sister’s son: See what you are asking me; tomorrow in the study hall…” And this is not ben Pedat, for ben Pedat is Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat.
tosafot:a12.2: Fetuses are not imbued with sanctity: that if he consecrated a fetus in the womb of its mother, a non-sacred animal, it is not sacred to be sacrificed. And if he sacrifices it when it is born and did not consecrate it once born, he is bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple courtyard. And if he separated a pregnant animal as a sin offering, they are not like two sin offerings set aside as a guarantee, for the fetus is sacred by force of its mother and not by its own force; it is like the offspring of a sin offering and goes to its death. And so in all its matters it is like the offspring of consecrated animals, and not like an original consecration.
tosafot:a12.3: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Fetuses are imbued with sanctity: if he consecrated a fetus in the womb of its mother, a non-sacred animal, it is sacred. And if he separated a pregnant animal as a sin offering, it is like one who separates two sin offerings as a guarantee, and the offspring is not like the offspring of a sin offering; rather, its sanctity is sanctity by word of mouth, by force of the person, and not by force of the mother. We find that the offspring of a sin offering goes to its death only where one consecrated a sin offering that was not pregnant and it then became pregnant.
tosafot:a12.4: In brief: “If he wishes he may achieve atonement through its offspring” means that the offspring needs no further consecration and it is like separating two sin offerings as a guarantee; this is why it shows that Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that sanctity takes effect on fetuses, for otherwise it would need another consecration once born. The proof cannot be that the offspring does not go to its death, since even if sanctity did not take effect on the fetus it would not die: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that if one excluded the fetus it is excluded, so that one may say of a non-sacred animal “it is sacred and its offspring non-sacred”, since a fetus is not the thigh of its mother (Temurah 25a). Tosafot then question Rashi’s explanation of bar Padda, that a pregnant sin offering’s offspring would go to its death: perhaps bar Padda too holds that if one excluded it, it is excluded? They answer that bar Padda must hold that it is not excluded, or the mishna on 24b (“it is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering: it is the offspring of a peace offering”) would be difficult for him, since he could have excluded the offspring; for Rabbi Yoḥanan the offspring is a peace offering by the person’s word, but for bar Padda it is sacred only through its mother. If you ask how, for bar Padda, “its offspring is a burnt offering and it is a peace offering” stands, the answer is that it speaks of sanctity of value. If you ask how one may consecrate a fetus at all, when one may not consecrate an animal whose time has not arrived, yet the mishna on the firstborn (24b) says “what is in its womb, if male, is a burnt offering”: before birth one may consecrate it, as Bekhorot (14a) derives from a verse. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: Does the one who consecrates add one-fifth or the one atoning add one-fifth: for example, where one person consecrated an offering to discharge the obligation of his fellow; if they wish to redeem it, the one who consecrated or the one atoning, which of them is obligated to add one-fifth?
gershom:a2.1: For example, where the community or partners appointed an agent and said to the agent: Go and consecrate an animal for us. If one who consecrates for another’s need effects substitution, this one who consecrated, who is an individual, would effect substitution too; but since they are many, they do not effect substitution.
gershom:a3.1: And furthermore, we hear it from what Rav Naḥman said etc. But is a nazirite judged according to his means? He has no sliding-scale offering! Rather, “his offering unto the Lord for his naziriteship” is what he attained from his own; “besides that for which his means suffice” is what others attained and separated for him from their own. With regard to what halakha does it say this? If with regard to atonement, that he can atone with an animal of others, it is obvious that it atones, since they are giving it to him as a gift. Rather, it says this with regard to substitution, and this is what it is saying: [even] where others separated it for him etc.
gershom:a4.1: What was concluded about it, for Rav Naḥman: come and hear what Rabbi Abbahu said etc. The benefit of discretion is the separator’s, for he may take a dinar from an Israelite in return for giving it to that man’s daughter’s son, a priest.
gershom:a5.1: One does not substitute limbs: [Rabbeinu Gershom reads it as] limbs of consecrated animals for fetuses of non-sacred ones, nor limbs and fetuses of consecrated animals for whole non-sacred animals, for the sanctity of substitution does not take hold of one limb alone while it is attached to the animal’s body, and he has said nothing. And likewise not whole animals for them. [Rashi reads it the other way: non-sacred limbs for consecrated fetuses.]
gershom:a6.1: Rabbi Yosei says: One substitutes limbs for whole animals: for he holds that since he said: Let the leg of this non-sacred animal be in place of this one, the sanctity of substitution spreads through the whole animal and it is a substitute, just like “the leg of this one is a burnt offering” etc. [The printed text reads “consecrated” and is corrected in brackets to “non-sacred”.]
gershom:a7.1: And not whole animals for them: for a non-sacred animal is not taken hold of by substitution through one limb of a consecrated animal or through a consecrated fetus, and he has said nothing. Ben Padda says: Sanctity does not take effect on fetuses: if someone said of a pregnant non-sacred animal: Let its fetus be sacred, sanctity does not take effect on it; and Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Sanctity takes effect on it. Another version: what is Rabbi Yoḥanan teaching us with “if he wishes he atones with it, if he wishes he atones with its offspring”? He teaches us that if one excluded the fetus, it is excluded; for example, where he said: It is a peace offering and its fetus a burnt offering, it is a peace offering and the fetus remains a burnt offering, since a fetus is not the thigh of its mother. Another reason it is excluded: because it is like one who separates two sin offerings as a guarantee, that if this one is lost the other will be in its place, and he atones with whichever he wishes. And this teaching of Rabbi Yoḥanan is also in the chapter Keitzad Ma’arimin al HaBekhor. And if you find it difficult from what we learned, “the offspring of a sin offering and the substitute of a sin offering are left to die”: there it is where he consecrated it and it later became pregnant, and here it speaks of where he consecrated it while it was pregnant.
rashi:b1.1: The fetus itself: by itself; therefore the sanctity takes effect on it.
tosafot:b1.1: But here, where he consecrated its mother, it is included in its mother: [one of the Tosafists, whose name is abbreviated in the text,] found it difficult: why do I need this argument of necessity? Let it say plainly: had Rabbi Yoḥanan taught us only the first case, I would say that if one excluded the fetus it is not excluded, and therefore he had to say “if he wishes he may achieve atonement through its offspring”, to teach that if one excluded it, it is excluded, as [Rashi] explained. And it is further difficult: how can it say that as part of its mother it is not sacred? We learned explicitly in Keitzad Ma’arimin (Temurah 25a): “It is a peace offering and its offspring a burnt offering: it is the offspring of a peace offering”, so evidently it is sacred as part of its mother! One can answer that this is its meaning: as part of its mother it is not sacred by the person’s word, but it is sacred by being carried by its mother, since a fetus is the thigh of its mother and if one excluded it, it is not excluded. Therefore it was necessary in the latter case to teach that the offspring is sacred by the person’s word and not by being carried by its mother. [Signed:] HaRam.
rashi:b3.1: Another version: What is Rabbi Yoḥanan teaching us? If he excluded it, it is excluded, and a fetus is not the thigh of its mother: since Rabbi Yoḥanan counts it in its own right, and not as the offspring of a sin offering that goes to its death, conclude that if he wished to exclude the fetus for another sanctity, it is excluded. For example, if he said: This shall be a sin offering and its fetus a burnt offering, his words stand, since a fetus is not the thigh of its mother; or if he excluded it by saying: It is a sin offering and its offspring is non-sacred, [so it is]. And bar Padda does not count the fetus as being in its own right: where he consecrated its mother and excluded the offspring for another sanctity, it is not sacred [as he said], but is the offspring of a sin offering and goes to its death; and if he said: Its offspring is non-sacred, he has said nothing. And according to the one who says that the offspring of consecrated animals are sacred in their mothers’ womb, it is sacred immediately; and according to the one who says that they are sacred when they come into being, it is sacred when it is born.
rashi:b3.2: And why do I need two etc.: we already heard it from the first, where he said that sanctity takes effect on fetuses; by implication the offspring counts as an animal in its own right.
rashi:b4.1: Fit for itself: for the mother is sacred with inherent sanctity, to be sacrificed.
rashi:b6.1: How may one employ artifice with the firstborn: to remove it from the priest and benefit from it himself.
rashi:b6.2: If it gave birth to a male, it is a burnt offering: and he sacrifices it for his obligation and fulfills it, if he was obligated to bring a burnt offering. For the sanctity of the burnt offering came first and takes effect on it, since by firstborn status it is not sacred until the womb sanctifies it [at birth]; and firstborn status then no longer comes and removes the sanctity of the burnt offering. Evidently a fetus becomes sacred, and this is difficult for bar Padda.
rashi:b7.1: Sanctity of value: that he sells it and brings a burnt offering with its value; but it itself is not sacred with inherent sanctity, rather it is sold without a blemish.
rashi:b8.1: And we learned: said as support [not as a question].
rashi:b8.2: They are obligated with regard to the firstborn: if they are females and gave birth to a firstborn after their redemption.
rashi:b8.3: [Evidently] sanctity of value is strong: for since the permanent blemish preceded the consecration, it was sacred from the start only for its value.
rashi:b9.1: Permitted: the mother, to be shorn, since he did not consecrate her body.
rashi:b9.2: Weakening of the fetus: for the mother’s labor weakens the fetus. Evidently the fetus is sacred.
rashi:b10.1: And we learned: said as support [not as a question].
rashi:b10.2: They emerge to non-sacred status: this is the latter clause of the mishna you cited above, “All sacrificial animals in which a permanent blemish preceded” etc., and it teaches in the latter clause: “They emerge to non-sacred status” when redeemed, “to be shorn and to be used for labor”, i.e., they are permitted to be shorn and used for labor after their redemption, since the permanent blemish preceded their consecration and they were not sacred with inherent sanctity. This is in the second chapter of Bekhorot (14a).
rashi:b11.1: He raised an objection: Rabbi Yirmeya to Rabbi Zeira.
rashi:b11.2: One does not substitute etc.: it is our mishna, and it teaches: “Nor whole animals for them.”
rashi:b11.3: It is substitution that one cannot effect: because with regard to substitution it is written “an animal for an animal”, and a fetus is not an animal.
rashi:b11.4: But if one consecrates them, they are consecrated: the fetuses. For if they were not sacred, it would be obvious that one does not substitute whole non-sacred animals for them.
tosafot:b7.1: When that mishna is taught, it is referring to sanctity of value: it is difficult: if so, what does the latter clause of that mishna in Keitzad Ma’arimin (below 24b) mean: “If it gave birth to two males, one of them shall be sacrificed as a burnt offering”? Since it has only sanctity of value, why is it sacrificed as a burnt offering? And if you say it means it is sold for the needs of a burnt offering, it teaches there: “And the second is sold for the needs of a burnt offering”; if so, what is the difference between the first and the second? One must say that since sanctity of value descended on the first, inherent sanctity descended on it as well.
tosafot:b11.1: It is substitution that one cannot effect, but if one consecrates fetuses, they are consecrated: for if they were not sacred, it would be obvious that one does not substitute whole non-sacred animals for them. And here he cannot answer that it is sanctity of value, as above, for such animals do not effect substitution.
rashi:b13.1: But isn’t it taught: The offspring does not render a substitute: rather, we must certainly be dealing with one who consecrates the offspring [directly], which counts as an original consecration [and this is difficult for bar Padda].
rashi:b14.1: It is Rabbi Yehuda: in the mishna [12a], Rabbi Yehuda says that the offspring renders a substitute.
tosafot:b14.1: In brief: Some books read here a longer objection: “If Rabbi Yehuda, how is the first clause to be understood…”, word for word as Rashi explains it below (on “If this mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda”), down to Rabbi Zeira’s answer of a limb upon which life depends and the derivation “an animal for an animal”; Tosafot quote it and say “thus far Rashi’s wording”. It seems to Tosafot that one need not read all this, since it implies the objection rests on Rabbi Yosei’s reply, “But isn’t it so with regard to sacrificial animals… the entire animal”, from which it follows that the first tanna agrees. But in the chapter Behema HaMakshe [Ḥullin 69b] there is another version: Rabbi Yosei is answering his own view, while the first tanna disagrees with him even at the start of consecration. If so, one can say that the mishna is Rabbi Yehuda. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b15.1: If Rabbi Yehuda: how is the first clause to be understood, which teaches that one does not substitute non-sacred limbs for whole consecrated animals? It implies that it is substitution that limbs cannot effect for a non-sacred animal, i.e., that the sanctity of substitution would take effect on the body of the animal through its limb that he substituted for a whole consecrated animal; but if one consecrates, limbs are consecrated at the start of consecration: if he consecrated one limb, the sanctity spreads through all of it. For this tanna holds this reasoning, since Rabbi Yosei responds to him: “But isn’t it so with regard to sacrificial animals, one who says: Its leg is a burnt offering, all of it is a burnt offering”, which implies that the first tanna concedes that at the start of consecration, if he consecrated one limb, the sanctity spreads through all of it. And Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yosei’s counterpart below in the baraita, says that at the start of consecration all of it is a burnt offering, and teaches us that with regard to substitution it is not so: either because he expounds “an animal for an animal”, or because he juxtaposes substitution to the animal tithe at the end of our chapter (13a): just as the tithe is an individual’s offering etc.; and from that very juxtaposition he derives that just as the tithe does not apply to limbs, so substitution does not apply to limbs. And so it is said in the chapter Behema HaMakshe (Ḥullin 69b).
rashi:b15.2: But doesn’t Rabbi Yehuda say: below in the baraita, that the sanctity does not spread through all of it.
rashi:b15.3: What are we dealing with here: where we inferred that, not through substitution, the whole animal becomes sacred through one limb.
rashi:b15.4: With a limb upon which life depends: as it says below that Rabbi Yehuda concedes with regard to something that would render it a tereifa, for example if he consecrated its legs from the knee upward: all of it is a burnt offering. But with regard to substitution it is not so, since we expound “an animal for an animal”. [The printed Rashi reads “we do not expound”; Tosafot’s quotation of this Rashi (on “It is Rabbi Yehuda”) reads “not so, since we expound”.]
rashi:b16.1: One consecrates limbs and fetuses: this is below in the second chapter (16b), “There is a stringency in sacrificial animals over a substitute”, which lists stringencies and teaches this one: one consecrates limbs and fetuses, but one does not substitute for them.
gershom:b1.1: Why do I need two? It is necessary etc. How may one employ artifice with the firstborn: to remove it from the priest.
gershom:b2.1: When that is taught, it is for sanctity of value: for what it teaches, that if it gave birth to a male it is a burnt offering, is not for its body itself, to sacrifice it, but to sell it and buy a burnt offering with its value. But the fetus is not sacred in its body. Is it so strong etc.
gershom:b3.1: He said to him: Yes, and we learned: All sacrificial animals in which a permanent blemish preceded their consecration etc. For these have only sanctity of value, and if they were not redeemed they are exempt from the firstborn.
gershom:b4.1: Rabbi Zeira said to him: In accordance with whom is this? For the offspring of sacrificial animals in their mothers’ womb do not effect substitution, but outside they do.
gershom:b5.1: It is Rabbi Yehuda, who says that the offspring renders a substitute. And in fact it speaks of fetuses of sacrificial animals.
gershom:b6.1: But doesn’t Rabbi Yehuda say that limbs are not consecrated: so that the whole animal be consecrated; therefore it does not effect substitution. And the first tanna, Rabbi Yosei’s disputant in our mishna, is Rabbi Yehuda, as he says in the baraita below. But Rabbi Yehuda concedes with regard to a limb upon which life depends, that if he consecrated it, he consecrated all of it. And in fact it speaks of offspring of sacrificial animals.
gershom:b7.1: He raised an objection: One consecrates limbs and fetuses. Evidently a fetus becomes sacred. This too speaks of offspring of sacrificial animals.
gershom:b8.1: If it speaks of offspring of sacrificial animals, why does it teach “one consecrates”? They are already sacred!
